# Part 1: Workflow Architecture

## 1.1 The five-pass workflow survey

A workflow you have not measured is a workflow you are guessing about. The method below is a **workflow survey**, and it is run in five passes because each pass can invalidate the one after it. Running them together produces a document that describes a process nobody performs.

**The decision rule: do not design anything until the fifth pass has told you what people actually do, because the first four passes describe the process the organization believes it has.**

| Pass | What it establishes | The artifact it produces | What invalidates the next pass if skipped |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1. Boundary** | Where the workflow starts, where it ends, what a single unit of work is | A case definition | Every number you collect afterward is per something undefined |
| **2. Discovery** | How the work is done, from four independent instruments | A step inventory with owners | You profile a process you have only heard described |
| **3. Profile** | Volume, variance, cycle time, touch time | A volume and variance table | You size and prioritize on anecdote |
| **4. Failure** | Exception rate, rework loops, escape rate | A failure map | You automate the happy path and inherit the exceptions |
| **5. Shadow** | The distance between the documented procedure and the observed one | A divergence list | You automate a process that exists only on paper |

### Pass 1: the boundary and the four units of analysis

Most workflow arguments are two people using the same noun for different objects. Fix the unit first.

| Unit | Definition | The question it answers | Where architects get it wrong |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Case** | One end-to-end instance of the work, from trigger to closure | What does the business count? | Counting tasks and calling them cases inflates volume by an order of magnitude |
| **Task** | One bounded piece of work performed by one actor in one sitting | Where does the effort go? | Treating a task as the case hides the queues between tasks |
| **Decision** | A point where the path forks and someone chooses | Where does judgment live? | Decisions embedded inside tasks are invisible in a task-level map, and they are exactly what you are deciding whether to delegate |
| **Handoff** | A transfer of the case between actors, systems or teams | Where does time go? | Handoffs are where cycle time accumulates and where accountability blurs |

Decompose every workflow at all four levels. A **case-level** view gives you volume and cycle time. A **task-level** view gives you touch time and cost. A **decision-level** view gives you the delegation candidates. A **handoff-level** view gives you the waiting, the rework and the accountability gaps. The delegation map of 1.3 is built at the decision level, not the task level, and a survey that never reaches decision level cannot produce one.

### Pass 2: the four discovery instruments

No single instrument sees the whole process. Each has a systematic blindness, and the blindnesses are complementary, which is why you use four rather than the one that is convenient.

| Instrument | What it is | What it sees that nothing else does | What it systematically misses |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Observation** | Sit with the person doing the work and record every action for a full case | The workarounds, the second screen, the spreadsheet nobody mentions | Rare cases. You will not observe the 2 percent exception in a two-day sitting |
| **Interview** | Structured conversation with performers, supervisors and downstream consumers | Intent, judgment criteria, the reasons behind the workarounds | People describe the process they are supposed to follow, not the one they follow. Systematic and unconscious |
| **Process mining** | Reconstruct actual paths from system event logs, with timestamps and actor identifiers | True volume, true cycle time, true path variance, true rework frequency | Anything done outside the instrumented systems, which is usually where the judgment is |
| **Artifact archaeology** | Read the outputs. Old cases, email threads, comment histories, redline chains, ticket notes | What was actually decided and on what basis, plus the real distribution of inputs | Speed. It tells you what happened, not how long it took or what it cost |

**The instrument pairing rule: process mining tells you what happened and observation tells you why, so a survey with only one of the two produces either numbers you cannot explain or explanations you cannot size.**

The interview is the instrument with the most method to it, and the method matters as much as the instrument choice; 1.2 gives the order in which to run the conversations and the anti-patterns that make the answers worthless.

### Pass 3: volume and variance profiling

Volume alone justifies nothing. Volume paired with variance selects the pattern.

| Measure | Definition | Why it is decisive |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Case volume** | Cases per period, with the peak-to-average ratio | Peak is what has to fit inside rate limits and reviewer capacity, not average |
| **Input variance** | How many distinct input formats and sources arrive | High input variance is the single strongest argument for a model over a parser |
| **Path variance** | How many distinct routes through the process are actually taken, and what share the top three cover | If three paths cover 90 percent, you have a deterministic process with a long tail, not a variable one |
| **Judgment variance** | How often two qualified performers reach different conclusions on the same case | The honest measure of judgment content. If experts disagree 30 percent of the time, no system will be 95 percent "correct" against a single ground truth |
| **Output variance** | How much the acceptable output differs case to case | Low output variance plus high input variance is the ideal AI shape: many ways in, one shape out |

Judgment variance is the measure almost nobody collects and it is the one that most often kills a business case. Collect it by giving five performers the same twenty historical cases and comparing. If they agree 98 percent of the time, the work is rule-governed and you are probably looking at deterministic automation. If they agree 60 percent of the time, your eval set has no ground truth and you need a rubric before you need a model.

### Pass 3, continued: cycle time and touch time

```
  CASE: supplier invoice exception, professional services firm
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  arrive  triage    wait     analyst   wait    approver   post
   |------|---------|--------|---------|-------|----------|----|
   0     4m        3.2d      22m      1.8d      6m        2m
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  cycle time  = 5.0 days        touch time = 34 minutes
  wait ratio  = cycle / touch  = 212 : 1
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  Reading: the process is 99.5% waiting. Halving touch time
  changes cycle time by 0.24%. The queue is the workflow.
```

**Cycle time** is trigger to closure in elapsed time. **Touch time** is the sum of active work. The **wait ratio** between them is the most diagnostic single number a survey produces, and it routinely decides whether an AI project is worth doing at all.

A high wait ratio means the constraint is queueing, batching or availability, not effort. Making a 22 minute analyst task into a 3 minute review task is real, but if the case still waits 3.2 days for triage, the business owner will report no improvement and cancel. In that shape the correct architecture is often not a better analyst step but an always-available first pass that eliminates the triage queue, which is a different design with a different value story.

A low wait ratio, say 3 to 1, means effort is the constraint and touch time reduction converts directly into capacity.

### Pass 4: exceptions, rework and escapes

Three failure numbers, and they are three different things.

| Number | Definition | What a high value implies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Exception rate** | Share of cases that leave the standard path | The standard path is narrower than the work. Automating only the standard path buys less than the volume suggests |
| **Rework rate** | Share of cases that return to an earlier step | A quality defect upstream. Automating the downstream step preserves the defect and multiplies it |
| **Escape rate** | Share of defective cases that reach the customer or the record undetected | The only number that tells you what error actually costs today, and therefore your true baseline |

Rework loops deserve to be drawn, not tabulated. Every loop has an entry condition, a detector and a cost, and the detector is where a control already exists. If a case bounces from approver back to analyst 18 percent of the time because the analyst omitted a required attachment, the AI opportunity is a completeness check at submission, not a drafting assistant. That is a five-line rule, and it is worth more than the model.

**The escape rate is your baseline.** The discovery question that does the most work is what a specific error costs (1.2), and the escape rate is the frequency term in that calculation. Without it, any accuracy target you agree is arbitrary. A system that is 94 percent correct is a catastrophe if the humans it replaces escape at 0.4 percent, and a triumph if they escape at 11 percent.

### Pass 5: the shadow process

**⧉ The single biggest risk in workflow analysis is the shadow process, because it is invisible to every artifact the organization will hand you and it is where the process actually lives.** The documented standard operating procedure describes an idealized path. The real process contains a spreadsheet the team maintains outside the system of record, a WhatsApp group used to chase approvals, a senior person who is consulted informally on anything unusual and a set of undocumented rules of thumb that are the actual decision criteria. Automate the documented process and you will ship something that fails on contact with the work, and the failure will be blamed on the model.

Four tells that a shadow process is operating:

| Tell | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| The system-of-record data is clean but the outcomes vary | Someone is making the real decision elsewhere and recording the result |
| A step has a suspiciously uniform duration in the logs | It is being batch-recorded after the fact, so the log timestamps are fiction |
| Everyone names the same person as the one to ask | Undocumented judgment is concentrated in one head, which is both the risk and the training data |
| There is a file share, spreadsheet or inbox nobody mentioned in the interviews | The real work product lives there |

Surface the shadow process without punishing it. It exists because the documented process was inadequate, and the workarounds usually encode genuine domain knowledge. The survey's job is to move that knowledge into the design, not to report it as non-compliance.

**Worked example, professional services.** A global consultancy surveyed its engagement letter process, documented as five steps and eight days. Process mining showed a median of 19 days across 1,400 cases a year, path variance of 31 distinct routes with the top three covering 46 percent and a rework rate of 27 percent. Observation found the shadow: partners maintained personal precedent folders and drafted from those rather than from the firm template, then risk review rewrote against the template, which was the rework loop. The wait ratio was 84 to 1. The initial proposal was a drafting assistant. The survey redirected it: the actual defect was that the firm template was three years stale and partners had rationally abandoned it. The intervention was a maintained clause library with an AI first pass that drafted from it and flagged partner deviations for risk review at draft time rather than after. Rework fell to 9 percent and cycle time to 7 days, and roughly half of that gain came from the clause library alone.

## 1.2 Discovery interviews

A discovery interview is a method rather than a conversation, and the method is what makes the answers usable: who you talk to, in what order and the one question that decides most of the design.

### The one question that does the most work

**What is the consequence of a specific error?** Not "how accurate does it need to be", which invites the answer "very", but "if it gets this particular case wrong, what happens, to whom and who finds out".

That question drives: whether human review is required, whether the control must be deterministic, which model tier is justified, what the latency budget can be, what the evaluation set must contain and whether the project is viable at all. No other discovery question has that reach.

### The interview order that works

The sequence is an argument, parallel to the four decisions of 2.1:

1. **The business owner first**, for the outcome and the metric. Without these, nothing else has a frame.
2. **The people who do the work today, second.** This is where you learn what the current error rate is, which nobody has usually measured and which is your baseline.
3. **Data owners third**, because what exists and in what condition constrains everything.
4. **Security, legal and compliance fourth**, once you have enough of a shape to ask specific questions. Going to them first produces generic answers; going with a data flow produces useful ones.
5. **Operations fifth**, because you are about to ask them to carry something.
6. **Finance last**, because by now you can size it.

Reversing the first two is the most common error and it poisons the survey, because once the sponsor has described the process, performers correct the sponsor's version rather than describing their own.

### The translation move: a preference is a signal, not a requirement

The interview order gets you to the right people. This is what to do with what they say, and it is the single most transferable technique in discovery. **Stakeholders speak in preferences. Designs are built against constraints. The work is converting the first into the second, in the room, before the conversation moves on.**

A stakeholder says the system should feel seamless. Written down as "seamless", that is not a requirement, it is the stakeholder's summary of an experience. **Treat every experience word as a signal that more discovery is needed rather than as something to record**: seamless, easy, fast, simple, intuitive, smooth. The list is short and it recurs.

The conversion runs on four follow-up questions, and any of them will do the work.

- **What would make it feel not seamless?** The most productive, because people describe failure more precisely than success.
- **What must the user never notice?**
- **What has to happen behind the scenes for this to hold?**
- **What must still be true when something goes wrong?**

Asked of "seamless", those questions typically return four different constraints in four different parts of the architecture: a latency ceiling the user should not perceive, a rule against re-entering data that already exists upstream, a requirement that exceptions route quietly to a person rather than surfacing a technical error, and a boundary that the workflow stays inside one application. **One preference, four constraints, each testable and bounded, each in a different section of the design.** That is why the word cannot simply be recorded.

#### The four categories a discovery statement has to be forced into

A vague statement usually hides answers in more than one of these. Working the categories explicitly is what stops a call ending with three of the four filled in.

| Category | What it captures | Why it needs asking |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **What the system must do** | The capabilities, expressed as business outcomes rather than features. Where the work Claude owns separates from the work that stays with an existing system or a person | Stakeholders volunteer this one unprompted, which is why it is the only one most calls cover |
| **What the system must not do** | Boundaries, prohibited actions, and the cases that must route to a human | **Stakeholders almost never volunteer these**, so they have to be asked for by name. The absence of this category is the most common defect in a requirements document |
| **What the system must cost** | The envelope in terms the stakeholder controls: a latency target, a per-interaction ceiling, a volume forecast | Cost stated as a constraint at intake is a design input. Cost discovered after build is a renegotiation |
| **What the system must prove** | The evidence the deployment has to be able to produce | In a regulated workflow this is a requirement, not a reporting preference, and finding it in discovery is far cheaper than finding it in legal review weeks later |

**The must-not-do and must-prove categories are where the expensive constraints hide**, and both are silent by default. A stakeholder describing a clinical workflow will mention the drafting and will not mention that a licensed clinician must authorize the output before it enters the record, because to them that is not a feature, it is simply how the work is done.

#### The output is a translation table, one row per item

Discovery produces an artifact, not a set of notes. Each item becomes a row with four columns, and the fourth is what makes the table worth building.

| Stakeholder statement, as said | Implied constraint | Required architectural decision | Assumption being documented |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| "We want this to feel seamless" | The experience stays inside an agreed latency budget, and failures must not expose internals or break the flow | A p95 latency target as a design constraint, plus a graceful failure state that stays internal | Assumes seamless means perceived responsiveness and continuity. Confirm |
| "It just needs to read the form and route it" | Routing may be a deterministic business rule the organization already owns | Claude extracts; the rule engine routes | Assumes routing logic is owned and maintained outside the model. Confirm the owner |
| "Clinicians will review the output anyway" | A licensed person must authorize before the output carries clinical, legal or financial consequence | A human authorization step as a mandatory gate, not an optional addition | Assumes review is an architectural gate rather than a courtesy. Confirm authority and timing |
| "We are in healthcare, so be careful with data" | The workflow probably carries a formal proof obligation | Audit trail and data-handling evidence as a day-one requirement | Assumes a covered workflow with a formal obligation. Confirm scope with compliance |

**Keeping the statement as said, in quotation marks, is not a stylistic choice.** It is what lets a later reader check the translation rather than inherit it. A row that records only the constraint has already merged the stakeholder's words with the architect's interpretation, and the interpretation is the part most likely to be wrong.

⧉ **The fourth column is the control, and its discipline is that a requirement traces to something a stakeholder actually said while an assumption does not.** An unsourced item in a requirements document is the dangerous kind, because nobody remembers deciding it and everybody assumes somebody did. The review that catches it is mechanical: take each line of the requirements document and point at the sentence in the discovery record it came from. A line nobody can source is either an assumption to be confirmed or an architect's preference wearing a requirement's clothes.

### Anti-patterns worth having a name for

| Anti-pattern | Why it is fatal |
| --- | --- |
| Accepting "we want to use AI" as a requirement | It is a preference for a technology, not a statement of a problem |
| Designing during the discovery meeting | The moment you start designing, discovery stops |
| Talking only to the sponsor | The sponsor knows what they want, not how the work is done |
| Never asking what happens when it is wrong | You will design as though errors are free |
| Not establishing the current baseline | You will be unable to demonstrate improvement, which is how successful projects get canceled |
| Not asking who signs off and what they need | You will build the thing and then discover you cannot ship it |

### Structured discovery

Who to talk to, and what each knows that nobody else does:

| Stakeholder | Their unique knowledge |
| --- | --- |
| Business owner | What outcome justifies the spend, and what success looks like |
| **The people who do the work today** | How it actually works, as opposed to how the process document says. Highest-value interview, most frequently skipped |
| Security | What boundaries exist, what review the design must pass, what will stop it reaching production |
| Legal and compliance | Which regimes apply, what data may be used for what, who is accountable |
| Operations | Who will run this, what they already carry, what an alert should do at 3am |
| Finance | The cost envelope |
| Data owners | What exists, where, in what condition, who may authorize its use |

What to extract is the nine-question list in 2.1.

### ⌂ The architect's lens

**The enterprise question this section does not ask.** What benefit is being claimed, who is accountable for delivering it and on what date will someone check whether it arrived? Sizing cost last produces a number, not a case.

**Governance at this decision.**

| Decision here | Governance decision that belongs with it | Artifact and owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Interviewing finance last | Quantified benefits, three-year cost including run and a named benefit owner | Business case, owned by the sponsor |
| Interviewing the people who do the work | Current-state map with volumes, cycle times, handoffs and rework rates | Process baseline, owned by the process owner |
| Interviewing data owners third | Assessing quality, lineage, licensing and the right to use the data | Data readiness assessment, owned by the data owner |
| Gathering requirements | Tracing each requirement to a design element, a test and an acceptance criterion | Traceability matrix, owned by the delivery lead |

**What this costs the organization.** Without a measured baseline the project cannot demonstrate improvement, and working systems get canceled in budget rounds for want of evidence. The forgotten cost is the benefits realization review after go-live: nobody schedules it, and its absence is why the next proposal is harder to fund.

**The executive translation.** Discovery delivers a funded business case with a named benefit owner and a date on which we test whether the benefit landed.

### From a business requirement to a scoped statement of work

A discovery interview produces material. It does not produce scope. The step between the two runs in four moves, and skipping any one of them produces a commitment that will not survive the next conversation with the business owner.

| Step | The move | What it produces |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1. Requirement to capability list** | "Process insurance claims" is a goal, not a capability. Name each capability separately: extract structured fields from the claim document, look up policy coverage, route to the adjuster queue by claim type and value, draft the adjuster notification | A list of capabilities, each nameable in one clause |
| **2. Capability list to architecture sketch** | For each capability decide where it belongs. Which does the model own, which belong to existing systems, which require a human in the loop. This is the delegation method of 1.3 applied to one use case | An assignment of every capability to an owner |
| **3. Architecture sketch to boundary conditions** | State the conditions under which the architecture works and the conditions under which it does not. An architecture that works for documents up to twenty pages and fails on longer ones has a boundary condition | A list of conditions, each with the failure that follows when it is violated |
| **4. Boundary conditions into the statement of work** | The conditions travel into the contractual scope, so the delivery team and the business owner both know what the system is designed to handle and what is explicitly out | A scope statement with the exclusions written down |

**The fourth move is the one that gets dropped, and it is the one that pays.** A boundary condition discovered in discovery and written into the statement of work is a scoping decision. The same condition discovered in production is a defect, and the argument about whether it was ever in scope is unwinnable in both directions.

⧉ **A capability list that names four capabilities and an architecture sketch that assigns three of them has not identified a gap; it has hidden one.** The unassigned capability is being performed by somebody, usually the user, usually unbudgeted, and it will appear in the cost model only after launch.


## 1.3 Delegation: the three owners and the mapping method

Decomposition produces a **delegation map**, and it answers the first of the four decisions (2.1): what part of the work Claude should own.

### The framing: delegation as a competency, not a step

For each part of the request you decide not just whether Claude *can* do it, but whether Claude *should own* it. **Can and should are separated**, and the whole discipline lives in the gap. And the outcome of the decision is not binary. Three outcomes:

| Outcome | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| **AI-appropriate work** | Claude owns it |
| **Human-retained work** | A person owns it, and Claude does not do it |
| **Collaborative work** | Claude drafts and a person decides. Claude produces, the human owns the decision |

The third row is the one most designs get wrong by collapsing it into the first. A draft that a person is expected to approve is a different artifact from an output that goes straight through, and it needs different plumbing: provenance, the ability to see the basis and a real point of refusal.

**The three justification criteria.** Every assignment is justified through three questions:

| Criterion | The question |
| --- | --- |
| **Reversibility** | Can a wrong call be undone? |
| **Stakes** | What does a wrong call cost? |
| **Accountability** | Who must answer for it? |

**⧉ The biggest risk in the triad is reading it as a single axis.** Reversibility and stakes are not the same axis: a cheap error that cannot be undone (a message sent to a client) and an expensive error that can (a miscalculated quote caught before issue) call for different designs. And accountability is a third axis independent of both, the criterion a technically minded architect is most likely to omit and the one a regulator will ask about first. Where accountability sits with a named person, the work is human-retained or collaborative regardless of how reversible or cheap the error is.

The instrument for the assignment is the four **behavior properties** of 2.2, which tell you what Claude can be trusted with. That section is not background: it is the lens through which every row of the delegation map is decided.

Delegation is also a competency in its own right, the first of the four in the **4D framework** published by Anthropic as its AI Fluency material and developed with Prof. Rick Dakan and Prof. Joseph Feller: **Delegation**, deciding what work to do with AI versus independently; **Description**, communicating effectively with AI; **Discernment**, critically evaluating outputs, processes and behaviors; **Diligence**, responsible and accountable use, including transparency. The same framework names three **modes** of working with AI: **Automation, Augmentation and Agency**. Do not map the modes onto the three solution patterns of 2.4: Automation, Augmentation and Agency are adjacent to Augmented LLM, Workflow and Agent but they are not the same taxonomy, and the resemblance is close enough to mislead.

### The three owners

Who does what? Every solution has three owners, and assigning them early sets you up for success. Every step of the work lands in one of three buckets:

| Owner | What belongs here |
| --- | --- |
| **What Claude does** | The work that benefits from language understanding, summarization, planning, drafting or tool-mediated action |
| **What existing systems do** | Anything the organization has already paid to make reliable: the order-status service, the policy engine, the rules table, the database of record |
| **What humans do** | The judgment calls, the exception paths, the approvals, the moments where being right matters more than being fast |

**The second owner is existing systems, not code, and the difference is not cosmetic.** "Code" invites you to think about what you will write. "Existing systems" points at what the organization already owns and has already paid to make reliable, named in four concrete instances: the order-status service, the policy engine, the rules table, the database of record. When a workflow already contains a policy engine or a system of record, the work belongs to that system, and any design that has Claude reproduce its logic is wrong.

**The question that operationalizes it: where does Claude do better than the system that already gets this right?** If there is no answer, the work stays where it is. The question puts the burden of proof on the model rather than on the incumbent system, and it disposes of most assignments in this family without further analysis.

Note the verbs assigned to Claude: language understanding, summarization, planning, drafting, **tool-mediated action**. Planning is on the list. So is acting through tools. The boundary is not "Claude only handles text."

And note the phrase in the third row: the moments where **being right matters more than being fast**. That is the cleanest available statement of when latency is the correct thing to spend, and it is a sentence worth being able to say to a client.

**The named failure: collapsing all three owners into "what Claude does".** Over-assigning tasks to Claude almost always makes the process **more expensive, slower and harder**. Three consequences, in that order, and the middle term is counter-intuitive: over-assigning to Claude makes the process *slower*, not faster, which is the opposite of the intuition that drives the mistake. The remedy is knowing what Claude does best and what it should be responsible for in the solution. Capability and responsibility, kept separate: the same can-versus-should distinction the delegation map exists to record.

### Worked scenario: decomposing a claims triage assistant

The request arrives as one sentence: a claims triage assistant that reads a claim, decides priority and looks things up along the way. Decomposed against the three owners: reading a claim is language understanding, so Claude. Deciding priority is a classification that controls downstream handling, so Claude may classify while an existing system or code routes. Looking something up is a system of record. And whatever the claim's disposition turns out to be, if it affects a payment or a denial it is human-retained or collaborative on accountability grounds alone. One sentence of request, all three owners present and accountability doing the decisive work at the end.

### Failure mode: deterministic drift

**Deterministic drift** runs in two directions and both are quiet. In the first, work assigned to Claude gradually takes over a job that a deterministic system should own, so that a process which is nominally rule-governed drifts into being model-governed. That is the delegation-level version of a failure that recurs in the reference architectures (2.5), retrieval quietly doing a job that the live transactional state should own, generalized one level up. In the second, a design assumes determinism where there is none, so that behavior drifts between runs while everyone treats the output as fixed. Both directions stay invisible for the reason 2.2 gives: the properties do not announce themselves.

Both land on the same control. **A rule that the business is counting on must be tested, watched and owned by a human.** The answer to drift is not a better prompt and not a stricter instruction: it is that the rule acquires an owner, a test and a watcher. The control holds whether what drifted is a rule, deterministic logic migrating into a model-owned step or a role, accountability going unassigned.

### Delegation mapping as a working method

**The mapping table.** A delegation map is a table with one row per step. The last two columns are what make it useful rather than decorative:

| Step | Nature of the work | Owner | Why | Failure mode if mis-assigned | Control |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Extract invoice fields from a PDF | Interpretation of unstructured input | Claude | No rule can express the variety of layouts | Existing system: brittle, fails on every new template | Schema validation; nullable fields; confidence routing |
| Verify the invoice total | Arithmetic | Existing system or code | Must be exactly right | Claude: plausible arithmetic errors that read as correct | Recompute and compare; flag mismatch |
| Check the vendor is approved | Lookup against a list | Existing system of record | Deterministic membership test | Claude: hallucinated approval | Hard gate before payment steps |
| Decide whether to pay above the threshold | Consequential financial decision | Human | Accountability and asymmetric cost | Claude: unauthorized payment | Approval gate; no tool that can execute without it |
| Draft the query to the vendor | Language | Claude, collaborative | Judgment about tone and content | Existing template that fits no actual situation | Human decides before sending |

**Five supplementary assignment tests**, subordinate to Reversibility, Stakes and Accountability:

1. **Is there a single correct answer expressible as a rule?** If yes, an existing system or code. This test alone resolves most steps and most people skip it.
2. **Is there a verifiable ground truth?** If yes, verification is available and should be built. If no, you need a rubric and sampled review instead, and you should know that before you build.
3. **Is the cost of a wrong answer symmetric?** Asymmetric costs, such as denying a valid claim versus approving an invalid one, push toward human involvement on the expensive side specifically, not on both. This is the Stakes criterion, sharpened.
4. **Who notices if this step is wrong, and when?** If the answer is "nobody, until the quarter closes," the step needs a control regardless of who owns it. Steps whose errors are invisible are the dangerous ones.
5. **Would a competent junior need judgment or a rulebook?** Rulebook means a system. Judgment means Claude, or a person if the judgment carries accountability.

**The reverse test, which is the part most delegation maps are missing.** For every step assigned to Claude, name the thing that verifies it. If you cannot, either add verification or move the step. A delegation map with unverified model-owned steps in a consequential path is not a design, it is a hope.

**Four boundary cases worth thinking through in advance**, because they are where mis-assignment hides:

| Case | The trap | The resolution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Classification that determines a routing decision | Looks like judgment, so it goes to Claude; but it *controls* a deterministic branch | Claude may classify; a system must route. And the classification needs measured accuracy, because branch errors are silent |
| Threshold checks stated in policy prose | The policy is language, so the whole thing feels like a language task | Claude may *find* the threshold in the policy; the policy engine must *apply* it |
| Summarization feeding a decision | Summarizing is clearly Claude's work | True, but the decision is downstream and the summary is now the evidence. This is collaborative work: preserve provenance, or the decision-maker cannot check the basis |
| Authorization expressed in natural language | The rule is written in prose, so prose seems the natural medium | Never. Authorization is deterministic by definition. Model reads, system enforces |

### Decomposition principles

Decomposition runs along four axes: **by subtask, by data slice, by pass, by expertise**. Two quality tests apply to any decomposition: **coverage**, does the union of subtasks cover the goal, and **non-overlap**, do any two duplicate each other.

The classic failure is a decomposition that is internally tidy and collectively incomplete. Splitting "impact of AI on creative industries" into three visual-arts subtasks produces three flawless subagent reports and one synthesis that never mentions music, writing or film. Coverage fails silently, because every part passes its own review.

### ⌂ The architect's lens

**The enterprise question this section does not ask.** The map assigns work to a category rather than a named role, and it never asks whether the humans it hands work to exist in sufficient number at expected volume.

**Governance at this decision.**

| Decision here | Governance decision that belongs with it | Artifact and owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Marking a step human-retained | Reviewer capacity, unit cost and queue service level at peak | Capacity plan and staffing model. Operations owner |
| Marking a step collaborative | How rubber-stamping is prevented, measured and evidenced | Reviewer procedure with sampling plan and override rate report. Operations owner |
| Assigning a step to Claude on stakes grounds | The threshold above which a named role must sign, and the exception path | Delegation of authority schedule with roles and thresholds. Accountable executive |

**What this costs the organization.** Moving work off people changes job descriptions, training, performance measures and in some jurisdictions consultation obligations, none of which appear in a delegation map. The cost people forget is the review queue: a design routing a fifth of volume to reviewers nobody hired fails at go live, and the field remedy is to skip the review under load.

**The executive translation.** This changes who is accountable for parts of a business process, so it needs the same signatures as any other delegation of authority change.

## 1.4 The seven-factor assignment score

Every step surveyed must be assigned to one of four destinations. This is the enterprise-scale version of the delegation map of 1.3, and it extends it, because at portfolio scale you need a score you can defend in a governance forum rather than a judgment you formed in a workshop.

**The decision rule: score need first, and if need is low the answer is deterministic code no matter how high the volume or how fashionable the program.**

### The seven factors

| Axis | Factor | 1 means | 5 means |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Need** | **Variance** | One input format, one path, fully structured | Many formats, unstructured, unpredictable phrasing |
| **Need** | **Judgment** | A written rule decides it and nobody disputes the rule | Experts disagree, the criteria are tacit, context governs |
| **Restraint** | **Reversibility** | Undone in seconds with no external effect | Irreversible: money moved, a filing made, a message sent to a client |
| **Restraint** | **Stakes** | Trivial if wrong | Regulatory, safety, financial or reputational consequence |
| **Restraint** | **Auditability** | Nobody will ever ask why | A regulator, auditor or court may require the reasoning to be reconstructed |
| **Restraint** | **Cost of error** | Cheap to detect and cheap to correct | Expensive to detect, and detection is late |
| **Worth** | **Volume** | A handful a year | Continuous, thousands per period |

Need = Variance + Judgment, range 2 to 10. Restraint = Reversibility + Stakes + Auditability + Cost of error, range 4 to 20. Worth is the volume factor read on its own.

### The routing table

| Need | Restraint | Destination | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2 to 4 | any | **Deterministic automation** | There is no variance for a model to absorb and no judgment for it to exercise. A model here adds cost, latency and non-determinism and buys nothing |
| 5 to 10 | 4 to 8 | **Agentic AI** | Real variance, low consequence. Let it run and sample the output |
| 5 to 10 | 9 to 14 | **AI with a human gate** | The model drafts, a person decides. The collaborative assignment of 1.3 |
| 5 to 10 | 15 to 20 | **Human, AI-assisted at most** | The accountability cannot be delegated and the audit requirement will not be satisfied by a probabilistic step |
| any | any | **Leave it human** if Worth is 1 to 2 | Below a volume floor nothing amortizes. Build nothing |

Two refinements. Volume never promotes a step across a restraint boundary; it only decides whether to build. And a high Restraint score does not forbid AI, it forbids AI owning the decision. The drafting can still be delegated when the deciding cannot.

### Worked examples across four functions

| Domain | Step | V | J | Need | R | S | A | E | Restraint | Destination |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Legal** | Extract parties, term and governing law from executed contracts | 4 | 2 | 6 | 2 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 9 | AI with a human gate on low confidence |
| **Legal** | Determine privilege over a document in discovery | 5 | 5 | 10 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 20 | Human, AI-assisted at most ⚠ |
| **Procurement** | Three-way match of invoice, purchase order and goods receipt | 1 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 13 | Deterministic automation |
| **Procurement** | Draft a supplier risk memo from filings, news and audit history | 5 | 3 | 8 | 1 | 3 | 3 | 2 | 9 | AI with a human gate |
| **Finance** | Post a recurring accrual from a fixed schedule | 1 | 1 | 2 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 4 | 17 | Deterministic automation |
| **Finance** | Assess revenue recognition on a multi-element arrangement | 4 | 5 | 9 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 20 | Human, AI-assisted at most ⚠ |
| **Customer ops** | Change of address on an authenticated account | 1 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 10 | Deterministic automation |
| **Customer ops** | Categorize an inbound complaint and draft a first response | 5 | 3 | 8 | 3 | 3 | 3 | 3 | 12 | AI with a human gate, sampled audit once calibrated |
| **Customer ops** | Determine that a customer is vulnerable and requires special handling | 4 | 5 | 9 | 4 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 19 | Human ⚠ |

Note the two finance rows. Both score 17 and 20 on restraint, which is high, and their destinations differ entirely, because need differs. Restraint tells you how much to constrain. Need tells you whether a model belongs there at all. Reading only restraint is how organizations end up gating a process that never needed a model, which is the worst of both outcomes: the cost of AI and the throughput of manual review.

### The AI costume

Most enterprise "AI opportunities" arriving through an intake process are deterministic automation opportunities in an AI costume. They are submitted as AI because AI has budget and integration work does not. An architect who cannot say no to AI is not an architect, they are a procurement channel.

**The five tells of a deterministic problem wearing an AI costume:**

| Tell | Why it is decisive |
| --- | --- |
| The rule can be written down completely and nobody disputes it | Need is low by definition. Judgment scored 1 |
| The inputs are already structured, or would be if one upstream form were changed | The variance is self-inflicted and cheaper to remove than to absorb |
| The output is consumed by a system, not read by a person | The receiving system requires exactness that a probabilistic step cannot guarantee |
| The stated accuracy target is 100 percent | A tolerable error rate of zero is a specification for code. Say so in the room |
| The whole business case is labor hours on a repetitive task with a stable format | Stable format means a parser. The labor is real and the instrument is wrong |

The professional move is not to reject the request. It is to re-scope it: return an integration and rules proposal that delivers the stated outcome faster and cheaper than the AI proposal, and reserve the AI budget for the steps that actually scored above 4 on need. This is a credibility engine. A center that occasionally ships a deterministic answer is trusted when it says a model is required.

**Worked example, financial services.** A retail bank's intake produced 43 candidate use cases in one quarter. Scored on the seven factors, 24 landed in deterministic automation, 11 in AI with a human gate, 5 in agentic AI and 3 were killed on the volume floor. The 24 were routed to the existing robotic process automation and integration team, which delivered 19 of them in two quarters. The AI team, freed of them, shipped 4 of the 11 gated cases in the same period, at a measurable quality baseline. The head of the program reported the deterministic 19 as program outcomes, which is correct: the program's job was the outcome, not the instrument.

## 1.5 Automate or redesign

Automating a process encodes it. Whatever was true about the process the day you automated it stays true permanently, and becomes harder to change than it was when it was manual. This is the **paving the cowpath** failure: an inefficient path worn in by historical constraints gets surfaced in asphalt and becomes the permanent route.

**The decision rule: before automating any step, ask which constraint made that step necessary, and if AI has relaxed that constraint, delete the step instead of automating it.**

### The five constraints AI relaxes

| Constraint | The pre-AI cost | What it made necessary | What relaxing it unlocks |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Cost of reading** | A person had to read every page to know what was in it | Triage queues, summaries written for someone else, sampling instead of full review | Full-population review instead of sampled review. Screening at intake instead of after assignment |
| **Cost of drafting** | A blank page cost an hour of a skilled person | Templates, boilerplate, "just use the last one" precedent copying | Drafting per case rather than per template. Genuine tailoring at volume |
| **Cost of a first pass** | Scarce expertise had to be spent on the first look | Batching, seniority-graded queues, long waits for a specialist | Always-available first pass. The specialist sees a prepared case, not a raw one |
| **Cost of translation** | Moving between formats, languages, systems or professional vocabularies needed a person | Handoffs that exist purely to reformat. Intermediary roles | Direct connection between parties who could not previously read each other |
| **Cost of consistency checking** | Comparing this case against a hundred prior ones was infeasible | Precedent that lived in individual heads. Inconsistency accepted as unavoidable | Consistency as a checkable property. Deviation flagged at draft time |

### The three constraints AI does not relax

| Constraint | Why it does not move | The design consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The cost of being wrong** | The consequence lives in the world, not in the system. A wrong filing costs what it costs regardless of what produced it | Error cost is exogenous. It sets the restraint score and no model improvement changes it |
| **The cost of accountability** | Someone must be answerable, and a model cannot be. Accountability is a property of persons and legal entities | Every gated step needs a named human owner. Delegating the work never delegates the answerability ⚠ |
| **The cost of trust** | Trust is earned by a track record over time and is lost faster than it is gained | Adoption is paced by evidence, not by capability. Rollout plans that assume instant trust fail on adoption, not on quality |

This asymmetry is the whole redesign argument. AI makes the production of work cheap and leaves the consequences of work exactly where they were. So the redesigned process should produce more work product earlier and concentrate scarce human attention on the consequence-bearing decisions, rather than distributing human attention evenly across a process that was designed when production was the bottleneck.

### The three cowpath tests

Apply to every step in the surveyed process.

1. **Does this step exist only because reading was expensive?** Triage, routing, sampling, summarizing for someone else, "flag it for the specialist." If yes, the step is a candidate for deletion rather than automation.
2. **Does this handoff exist only because the two parties could not read each other's format?** Rekeying, reformatting, translation, "the ops team turns the email into a ticket." If yes, connect the parties and delete the intermediary step.
3. **Does this queue exist only because a first pass was scarce?** Any queue whose service time is minutes and whose wait is days. If yes, the queue is a scheduling artifact of scarcity that no longer exists.

A step that survives all three tests is a genuine step and can be automated in place. A step that fails one should be redesigned out, and automating it instead permanently entrenches a constraint you have already removed.

**Worked example, healthcare.** A hospital network's prior authorization process had six steps and a 9 day median. The AI proposal was to draft the authorization letter, which was step 5 and took a coordinator 25 minutes. Applying the cowpath tests: step 2, a coordinator reading the chart to determine which payer policy applied, existed only because reading was expensive. Step 3, a queue for a clinical reviewer to confirm the indication, existed only because a first pass was scarce. The redesign moved the policy determination and evidence assembly to an AI first pass at the point the order was placed, delivering the clinical reviewer a prepared packet with the policy criteria and the supporting chart excerpts already cited. Steps 2 and 3 collapsed into the order entry moment. Median fell to 2 days. The letter drafting, the original proposal, contributed less than a day of that. Had the team automated only step 5 they would have paved a six-step cowpath and reported a 1 day improvement.

## 1.6 Operating model engineering

Capability has to sit somewhere. Where it sits determines what gets built, how fast and how consistently, and the choice is usually made by accident when the first team hires the first person.

### The three operating shapes

| Shape | Where capability sits | Optimizes for | Costs you | Characteristic failure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Centralized** | One team owns all AI delivery | Consistency, standards, scarce skill leverage, governance | Throughput and domain depth. Every business unit queues | Becomes a bottleneck, then a tollbooth, then routed around |
| **Federated** | Each business unit builds its own | Speed, domain fit, ownership, adoption | Duplication, inconsistent controls, no reuse, seven versions of the same retrieval layer | Governance discovers the estate during an incident |
| **Hub and spoke** | A central platform and standards team, delivery embedded in units | Both, if the split is drawn correctly | Coordination overhead and a genuinely hard boundary decision | The hub tries to do delivery, becomes centralized and the spokes go quiet |

**The decision rule: centralize what must be identical everywhere and federate what must be close to the work, and if you cannot say which side a capability falls on, it belongs to the spokes until it has three consumers.** Two counts appear in this section and they answer different questions: **two consuming teams is what makes a team a platform team**, and **three consumers is what makes a capability worth moving to the hub**. Neither is the trigger for a specific shared service, which 2.10 sets service by service, and a few of those are day one regardless of consumer count.

```
  HUB AND SPOKE, drawn as an obligation boundary
  ------------------------------------------------------------
                     +--------------------------+
   MANDATORY  ---->  |  gateway | audit sink |   |   the hub
   (the waist)       |  identity | egress policy |   owns and
                     +--------------------------+   operates
                                 |
        +------------------------+------------------------+
        |                        |                        |
   +---------+             +---------+              +---------+
   | Legal   |             | Claims  |              | Supply  |
   | spoke   |             | spoke   |              | spoke   |
   +---------+             +---------+              +---------+
   own prompts,            own prompts,             own prompts,
   own evals,              own evals,               own evals,
   own corpus              own corpus               own corpus
  ------------------------------------------------------------
  Rule: the hub owns what an auditor would want to be uniform.
  Everything a domain expert would want to tune stays in a spoke.
```

### The center of excellence and its four failure modes

A **center of excellence** is a legitimate structure and it fails in four recognizable ways. Name them in advance and you can design against them.

| Failure mode | What it looks like | The tell | The correction |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **The bottleneck** | Every request queues behind the center's capacity | The intake backlog grows monotonically | Move delivery to spokes. The center keeps standards, platform and review |
| **The ivory tower** | Beautiful standards nobody uses, produced by people who have not shipped | Standards documents outnumber production systems | Require the center to run at least one production system it is accountable for |
| **The demo factory** | A stream of impressive prototypes, none in production | High pilot count, near-zero production count, no operational owners named | Change the success metric from pilots launched to systems in production with a named owner at 90 days |
| **The tollbooth** | Mandatory review with no service level and no delivery help | Business units start building outside the process and hiding it | Publish a review service level and pair every mandatory gate with a service the center actually provides |

The tollbooth is the most damaging because it produces a shadow estate, which is the operating-model version of the shadow process, and it is discovered the same way: during an incident.

### Platform team versus embedded team

Two different jobs, two different success metrics, and conflating them is the most common structural error.

| | Platform team | Embedded team |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Owns** | Shared services, standards, the asset library, the eval harness, the gateway | A specific business workflow end to end |
| **Success metric** | Time from approved idea to first production request, across the portfolio | Outcome on their workflow: cycle time, escape rate, cost per case |
| **Fails by** | Building for imagined consumers, shipping abstractions nobody asked for | Building a bespoke stack that duplicates the platform and cannot be operated by anyone else |
| **Reports to** | Engineering or the center | The business unit, with a dotted line to the center |
| **Staffing rule** | Small, senior, ruthless about scope | Domain-heavy, paired with one platform engineer |

**The rule: a platform team must have at least two consuming teams before it is a platform team, and until then it is an embedded team with ambitions.**

### The intake and prioritization funnel

```
  INTAKE FUNNEL, five gates, each one able to end the process
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
   requests in
       |
  [1] PROBLEM        outcome, consumer, error cost, baseline,
       |             success metric, sign-off owner
       v             -> rejected: "we want to use AI"
  [2] ASSIGNMENT     seven-factor score per step
       |             -> routed out: deterministic automation
       v
  [3] FEASIBILITY    data exists? volume? cost per outcome at 3x?
       |             -> killed in week one, not month six
       v
  [4] GOVERNANCE     route, residency, regime, egress. RULE-OUT
       |             -> killed before any cost or latency work
       v
  [5] PORTFOLIO      reuse of existing assets, named production
       |             owner, capacity in the operating plan
       v
   build queue
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  Gate 4 runs before cost and latency are weighed, never beside.
```

Gate 4's position is doctrinal: governance and regulated-industry constraints are a rule-out filter applied before cost and latency, not a factor weighed alongside them. A funnel that costs a design and then discovers the route is unavailable has wasted the design.

Gate 5 is the one most organizations lack, and it is the difference between a program and a pile. It asks whether this system will reuse the portfolio's existing assets, who operates it once live and whether that person has capacity. A system with no named production owner is not approved, it is deferred.

### The estate that never reaches intake

The funnel above governs work that arrives as a request. Most of the governed population does not arrive that way. It arrives as a **feature toggled on in software the enterprise already bought**, or as a **tool an individual adopted without asking**. Neither passes a gate, neither appears in a build queue and both are in production by the time anyone draws the architecture.

The two populations are different problems, and the difference decides the response.

| Population | How it arrives | Who decided | What the organization can actually do |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Embedded vendor capability** | A summarization, drafting or classification feature ships inside a suite, a CRM, a ticketing system or an HR platform, enabled by default or by an administrator who read a release note | The vendor, and then a system administrator with no risk mandate | Configure, tier, restrict or disable. The design itself is not negotiable |
| **Individually adopted tools** | A person signs up with a work address or a personal one and pastes work into it | An employee solving a real problem faster than the organization could | Sanction it, replace it or stop it. All three require finding it first |

The first is a **procurement and configuration problem** wearing an AI costume. There is already a contract, a vendor relationship and usually a renewal date, which means there is leverage and an owner. The second is an **adoption problem**: no contract, no owner, no logging and frequently no way to establish what left the building. The first is normally larger by volume of data and the second is normally larger by number of instances. Treating them as one category produces a policy that bans the second and never notices the first, which is the common shape and the wrong one.

**Discovery, and none of it can rest on self-declaration.** Asking business units to declare their AI systems finds the systems that were going to be declared anyway.

| Method | What it finds | Its limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Contract and renewal review** | AI features and AI clauses in software already bought. The renewal calendar is the work plan for this population, because renewal is the moment terms can actually change | Finds capability rather than use. A feature named in the contract may be switched off |
| **Expense and procurement data** | Corporate card and expense claims for individual subscriptions, and departmental purchases sitting below the threshold that triggers review | Misses free tiers, which is where most individual adoption lives |
| **Network and identity telemetry** | Egress to known AI service domains, and single sign-on or OAuth grants to third-party applications. The identity log is usually the highest-yield source in the estate | Finds destinations rather than content. Encrypted traffic says nothing about what was sent |
| **The survey question that works** | Asks people **what they use** for a named task rather than whether they use anything. "Which tools help you draft a first response to a customer complaint" gets answers. "Do you use unapproved AI tools" gets none | Self-reported, so it corroborates the other three rather than standing alone |

Run all four. Each one is weak by itself and the overlaps are what make the resulting inventory credible.

**Assessing an embedded vendor feature is a shorter job than assessing a build**, and knowing why keeps it short: the design decisions were made by someone else and are not open to you. There is no pattern to choose, no context strategy to set and no delegation map to draw. Five questions remain.

1. **Data flow.** What leaves the tenant, to whose infrastructure, in which region and whether the feature calls a subprocessor the contract does not name.
2. **Retention.** How long the vendor holds inputs and outputs, and whether that is configurable or fixed.
3. **Training use.** Whether customer data trains the vendor's models, whether an opt-out exists and whether it is currently on. ⚠ Whether a given setting satisfies a particular regime is a determination for counsel rather than for the administrator who read the toggle.
4. **Tiering.** What the feature can reach and change, rather than what it is advertised for. This is the ordinary rule for tiering something the organization did not commission (4.2).
5. **Can it be turned off**, by whom, at what granularity and does the setting survive the vendor's next release.

Answer those five and the feature is acceptable as configured, acceptable after a configuration change or not acceptable. The last case is a contract conversation with a date on it, not an engineering one.

**Regularizing a system found already running** follows one route whichever population it came from. Tier it **by capability rather than by intent**: what it can reach, what it can change and whose data it holds set the tier, and the fact that someone meant it as a personal productivity aid sets nothing. Then take an explicit keep-or-stop decision, because the failure mode here is the tolerated indefinite middle. If the decision is stop, the work is migration and revocation, and someone still has to own the need it was meeting or it returns under a different name. If the decision is keep, it enters the estate at the same evidence standard as anything commissioned: a named owner, a tier, logging to the central sink, an eval wherever the output is relied on and an entry in the dependency register. Keeping it is not an amnesty for the system. It is adoption, with the bill attached.

**The governance point that decides whether any of this is still true a year later: an inventory nobody can be punished for adding to is the only kind that stays current.** If registering a tool somebody adopted without approval starts a disciplinary process, registration stops and the inventory quietly becomes a list of the already compliant. Amnesty for the disclosure and accountability for what happens after it is the only combination that keeps an inventory alive, and it has to be stated by someone senior enough for people to believe it.

⧉ **The largest risk here is that the unregistered estate is discovered by someone else first.** A regulator, an auditor, a customer's security questionnaire or a journalist establishes the organization's AI footprint before the organization does, and it learns the size of its own estate from a party with standing to act on it. Every other cost in this subsection is recoverable on the organization's own schedule. That one arrives with a deadline, a written record and no architectural options left, because at that point the question is no longer what the estate should look like but why nobody knew.

### Standards versus autonomy

The governing idea is a **thin waist**: a small mandatory set that everything must pass through, and wide freedom above and below it.

| Layer | Posture | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Mandatory** | Non-negotiable, enforced technically rather than by policy | Traffic through the gateway, audit logging to the central sink, identity and secrets handling, data egress boundaries, the eval gate before production, the model dependency register entry |
| **Recommended** | Defaults you get for free, deviation allowed with a written reason | Prompt structure, retrieval layer, review interface, ADR template, asset naming |
| **Free** | Team's choice, no review | Prompt wording, domain rubrics, eval content, orchestration detail inside the system |

**The rule: make mandatory only what an auditor would expect to be uniform across the estate, and make everything a domain expert would want to tune free.** Each addition to the mandatory list has to be paid for in adoption, so the list should be short enough to recite from memory.

### Chargeback and funding models

| Model | How it works | Behavior it produces | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Central subsidy** | The center pays for everything | Fast adoption, zero cost discipline, an unmanageable bill in year two | The first year only, deliberately time-boxed |
| **Showback** | Costs attributed and reported, not billed | Awareness without friction. Usually the right middle | Years one to two, while unit economics are still being learned |
| **Chargeback** | Business units billed for actual consumption | Real cost discipline, and the first serious conversation about cost per completed outcome | Once cost per outcome is measurable and attributable |
| **Capital project** | Each system funded as a discrete investment | Rigor per system, no funding for shared platform work | Large single systems. Fatal as the only model, because nobody funds the gateway |

The failure to watch is funding delivery through capital projects and leaving the platform unfunded. The platform then gets built as a side effect of whichever project happened to need it first, in that project's shape, and every subsequent project inherits it.

### The five-stage capability maturity progression

| Stage | The tell | What you can promise | The trap |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1. Ad hoc** | Individuals using AI, nothing inventoried | Nothing | Believing the absence of incidents is evidence of safety |
| **2. Piloted** | A handful of projects, each with its own everything | A demonstration | Counting pilots as outcomes |
| **3. Platformed** | Shared gateway, logging and identity. Reuse begins | A repeatable delivery time | Building the platform before there are two consumers |
| **4. Governed** | Standards enforced, evals gate production, inventory complete, dependencies registered | A quality commitment with a metric and a population | Governance without delivery help, which produces the tollbooth |
| **5. Portfolio-managed** | Systems retired as well as launched, model migrations planned, capability decisions made against a portfolio view | A cost per outcome and a roadmap | Assuming the estate is stable. Model deprecation resets it |

**The rule: you cannot skip stage 3, because governance without a platform is policy, and policy that cannot be technically enforced is documentation.**

**Worked example, manufacturing.** A diversified manufacturer ran federated for eighteen months and accumulated 31 AI systems across 6 divisions. An inventory found 5 separate retrieval implementations, 4 vendors, 11 systems with no logging and 3 sending engineering drawings to an external service with no agreement in place. The correction was hub and spoke with a deliberately thin waist: gateway, audit sink and identity mandatory, everything else recommended. Migration took two quarters and the hub funded the engineering. The divisions kept their prompts, their evals and their domain corpora, which is why the migration succeeded. An earlier attempt to also centralize prompt authoring had been abandoned after the divisions simply stopped submitting work.

### ⌂ The architect's lens

**The enterprise question this section does not ask.** The funnel governs what arrives as a request. Nothing in it says who may decide that a system already running in production is allowed to continue, on whose authority, or by what date.

**Governance at this decision.** Three rows, and the block deliberately stops there. **The operating shape and the funding model are already owned in 7.5's block**, as the target operating model and the chargeback or showback model, and detecting unsanctioned tool use is 7.5's security row. **The gateway's own control design is 3.7's** and the audit sink's retention and access are 8.5's. Restating any of them here would put two owners on one artifact.

| Decision here | Governance decision that belongs with it | Artifact and owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Leaving an embedded vendor AI feature enabled | Whether the data flow, retention, training use and off switch are acceptable as configured, and by which renewal date the terms must change if they are not | Vendor AI feature assessment with a configuration position and a renewal date. Contract owner with the AI governance lead |
| Regularizing a system found already running | Keep or stop, with a date, and a tier set by what the system can reach and change rather than by what it was meant for | Estate register entry with tier, named owner and decision date. AI governance lead |
| Asking people to declare what they use | What registration triggers and what it does not, stated by someone senior enough that people believe it | Written disclosure position with the accountability that attaches after registration. Accountable executive |

**What this costs the organization.** An inventory is a standing cost, not a project: someone reconciles it against contracts, identity logs and expense data on a cycle, and the cycle is what keeps it true. The cost people forget is the tolerated middle, where a system found in discovery is neither adopted nor stopped, accrues users for a year and is then too embedded to remove and too undocumented to defend.

**The executive translation.** We do not yet know the size of our own AI estate, finding out is cheaper than being told, and the disclosure has to be safe to make or we will be told.

## 1.7 Reusable workflow assets

An asset library is what converts delivery into capability. Without it every project starts from zero and the organization gets slower as it grows, because more systems means more surface and no more leverage.

### The five asset types

| Asset | What it is | Who reads it | When | Failure when misused |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Playbook** | How to handle a class of situations where judgment is retained. Positions, fallbacks, criteria, escalation triggers | The person doing the work, and the model when it drafts | Before and during the work | Written as a procedure, so it becomes brittle and is ignored on the first unusual case |
| **Runbook** | Exact steps for a known operational condition, no judgment required | Operations, often at 3am | During an incident | Written with judgment in it, so it cannot be executed by someone who lacks context |
| **Template** | A skeleton for an artifact to be produced | Whoever produces the artifact | At production time | Confused with a standard. A template constrains shape, not content |
| **Pattern** | A named solution shape with its forces, trade-offs and known failure modes | Architects | At design time | Treated as a mandate rather than a shape with conditions of use |
| **Standard operating procedure** | The mandated sequence, with compliance force and an audit trail | Performers and auditors | Always, and deviation is an exception to be recorded | Used where a playbook is needed, which drives the real process into the shadow |

**The distinguishing rule: a runbook says what to do, a playbook says how to decide, a template says what to produce, a pattern says why the shape works and a standard operating procedure says what you are obliged to do.**

The playbook is the asset type that matters most for AI systems, because a playbook is exactly the artifact a model can be given as context. A good negotiation playbook, clause library or triage playbook is simultaneously a human enablement asset and the grounding for the model. Organizations that already maintain playbooks have a large head start and usually do not know it.

**These five are the reuse library's cut and they are not the only cut of the same material.** 5.5 names eleven asset types on a different axis, how each behaves when a model consumes it, and the two lists agree wherever they overlap. Use the five here to decide what belongs in the library, how it is versioned and when a one-off is promoted; use 5.5's eleven to decide what a retrieval system is allowed to do with a document once it is there. **5.6 gives the playbook and the runbook their executable structure**, which is what the library stores rather than what this section describes.

### The asset lifecycle

| Stage | Owner | Gate | What goes wrong without the gate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Author** | The team that needed it | It must state the problem it solves and the conditions under which it applies | Assets with no scope get applied where they do not fit |
| **Review** | A named reviewer outside the authoring team, plus subject matter and, where relevant, legal or compliance | Correctness, scope, no embedded confidential or client-specific content | Client-specific facts leak into a shared asset. This is a live incident category ⚠ |
| **Publish** | Library owner | Metadata complete, discoverable, licensed for its stated scope | An asset nobody can find is not an asset |
| **Version** | The authoring team | Semantic version, changelog and the eval set re-run if the asset is consumed by a system | A silently edited prompt asset breaks every system that consumed it, with no signal |
| **Deprecate** | Library owner | A stated replacement or a stated reason, a sunset date and notification of every registered consumer | Deprecated assets stay in production for years because nobody knew who was using them |

Deprecation is the stage everyone skips and it is the one that determines whether the library stays trustworthy. A library where a third of the assets are stale is worse than no library, because it degrades trust in the two-thirds that are current.

### Naming and metadata conventions

Naming is not cosmetic. It determines whether an asset is found at the moment it would have been useful, and an asset that is not found at that moment does not exist.

| Field | Why it is required |
| --- | --- |
| **Identifier** | Stable across renames. Referenced by systems, decision records and evals |
| **Type** | One of the five. Prevents a playbook being executed as a runbook |
| **Domain and scope** | The function and the process class it applies to |
| **Jurisdiction or entity scope** | The single most consequential metadata field in a regulated group. An asset valid in one entity may be non-compliant in another ⚠ |
| **Owner** | A named person, not a team mailbox. Teams do not answer questions |
| **Status** | Draft, published, deprecated, superseded |
| **Version and changelog** | So a consumer can tell whether their copy is current |
| **Model dependency** | Which model and version the asset was authored and evaluated against, if any |
| **Eval set reference** | The set that demonstrates the asset works, which is what makes it reusable rather than merely reused |
| **Review date** | Next review due. Assets rot silently |
| **Supersedes and superseded-by** | Makes the deprecation stage executable |

Name assets after the work, not the technology. `contract-nda-firstpass-playbook` survives a model change. `claude-nda-prompt-v3` does not, and it also tells a reader nothing about when to reach for it.

### The rule of three and where it fails

**The rule of three: promote a one-off into a reusable asset the third time it is needed, and not before.** Before three you are generalizing from insufficient evidence and you will build the wrong abstraction. The first two uses are how you learn what actually varies.

Four places the rule fails:

| Failure case | Why the rule breaks | What to do instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **High stakes, low volume** | Waiting for three occurrences means two of them were done without the control | Promote at the first use. Volume is not the criterion when the error cost is severe |
| **Regulated divergence** | Three uses look alike but sit in different jurisdictions or legal entities. Promoting produces one asset that is subtly wrong in two of them | Promote per scope, with jurisdiction as first-class metadata, or do not promote ⚠ |
| **Three uses by one person** | That is one use repeated, not evidence of generality. The abstraction encodes one person's habits | Require three distinct owners, not three occurrences |
| **Cheap re-derivation** | Some assets cost more to maintain, version and review than to rewrite each time | Never promote. A library of trivial assets buries the load-bearing ones |

**Worked example, financial services.** A bank promoted a know-your-customer refresh playbook to shared status after it was used three times in one region. Two other regions adopted it. Nine months later an internal audit found that the shared playbook encoded the first region's enhanced due diligence thresholds, which were stricter than one region's requirement and materially looser than another's. The asset was correct in one of three places. The fix was structural rather than editorial: the playbook was split into a shared core with the reasoning and process, plus a per-entity threshold appendix owned by that entity's compliance function, with jurisdiction added as a required metadata field for every asset in the library. ⚠ Threshold content of this kind is a regulatory determination and belongs with the accountable compliance owner, not with the architecture team.

## 1.8 Production readiness as an architectural checklist

Production readiness is not a phase at the end. Each property below is either designed in at a specific decision point or bolted on afterward at several times the cost, and three of them defeat a retrofit: one cannot be recovered at all, one can only be recovered by reconstruction that is itself a disclosable event, and the third can be added and is worthless when it is.

**The decision rule: for each of the nine properties, name the design decision that establishes it, and if the answer is "we will add it before launch," it will not be there.**

| # | Property | The question it answers | Established at | The bolt-on that fails |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Measurability** | Is there an eval set, a score, a baseline and segment-level breakdown? | Before the first prompt is written | An eval set built after launch is written against current behavior, so it certifies what the system already does |
| **2** | **Reversibility** | Can every action the system takes be undone, and in what time? | At the assignment decision, per step | Adding an undo path after the integration is built usually means the downstream system has no undo |
| **3** | **Observability** | Can operations reconstruct what happened on request X without redeploying? | At the integration design, with trace identifier, per-request identity and model identifier | Logging added later lacks the correlation identifiers, so events cannot be joined |
