| **4** | **Containment** | What is the blast radius of a wrong output, and how many cases before detection? | At the pattern and tool scope decision | Rate limits and kill switches added later do not reduce privilege, they only slow its exercise |
| **5** | **Accountability** | Who is answerable for each output, and do they know? | At the human oversight placement | An owner named at launch has not agreed to anything |
| **6** | **Portability** | What happens when the model is deprecated, and who owns the migration? | At the model selection decision, recorded in the dependency register | Discovered at the deprecation notice, with no runway |
| **7** | **Auditability** | Can the basis for a decision be reconstructed for a regulator or a court? | At the context and logging design ⚠ | Cannot be bolted on. If the inputs were not retained, the reasoning is unrecoverable |
| **8** | **Deletability** | Can an erasure request be satisfied across chunks, embeddings, caches, logs, memory and eval sets? | At the data map, before the first ingestion | Cannot be bolted on cheaply. Derived artifacts must be tracked from the start |
| **9** | **Operability** | Could a competent stranger operate, diagnose and change this? | Continuously, through decision records and a runbook | Documentation written at handoff records what was built and not why |

Property 7 is the one that cannot be recovered at all: if the inputs were not retained, no later work reconstructs the reasoning. Property 8 can be recovered, and the worked example below is what recovery costs, six weeks of engineering and a disclosure to the client, which is a different thing from a bolt-on. Property 1 is the one whose retrofit is worthless while looking complete. Those three are where architectural attention belongs at design time.

**This checklist is the design-time form of the readiness gate in 8.1, and the two do not cover the same ground.** 8.1 asks at launch, in eight evidenced dimensions with five signatories, whether the properties are present; 1.8 asks at each design decision whether they are being established. Seven of the nine map onto a gate dimension: measurability onto Evaluation, observability and operability onto Operational, containment onto Security, accountability onto the signatory set, auditability and deletability onto Governance. **Two do not appear on the gate at all.** Reversibility in 8.1 means rollback of a deployment, not undo of an action the system has already taken in a downstream system, and portability has no dimension: 8.1's Change dimension gates changes rather than planning a model deprecation. A team that passes the gate has not answered properties 2 and 6, so both have to be carried by the decision record and the dependency register rather than by the readiness review.

**Worked example, legal.** A law firm deployed a document review assistant and passed every readiness item except property 8. Eighteen months later a client terminated the relationship and exercised a contractual right to have its data returned and destroyed. The source documents were deleted. The chunk store, the embedding index, the prompt cache, the request logs and, most awkwardly, the eval set built from real matter examples all still held client content. Reconstructing what had to be deleted took six weeks of engineering and a disclosure to the client. The data map that would have prevented it would have taken two days at design time.

## Workflow Architecture: the one-page version

1. Run five passes: boundary, discovery, profile, failure, shadow. The fifth one governs, because the documented process is not the process.
2. Decompose at four levels: case, task, decision, handoff. The delegation map is built at decision level.
3. Use all four discovery instruments. Process mining says what happened, observation says why, interviews say what people believe and artifacts say what was actually decided.
4. Interview in order: the business owner first, then the people who do the work, then data owners, then security, legal and compliance, then operations, then finance. The one question that does the most work is what a specific error costs. Convert every preference into a constraint in the room, force each statement into what the system must do, must not do, must cost and must prove, record the statement as said so a later reader can check the translation, and carry the boundary conditions into the statement of work, because the same condition found in production is a defect and the argument about scope is unwinnable in both directions.
5. Profile five measures: case volume, then input, path, judgment and output variance. Judgment variance is the one nobody measures and the one that most often kills the business case.
6. Compute the wait ratio. A high one means the queue is the workflow and touch-time savings will not be visible.
7. Get the escape rate. It is your baseline, and without it every accuracy target you agree is arbitrary.
8. Assign every step to one of three owners: Claude, existing systems or humans. Justify each assignment on reversibility, stakes and accountability, and never let Claude reproduce what an existing system already gets right.
9. Score every step on seven factors. Need is variance plus judgment, restraint is reversibility plus stakes plus auditability plus error cost, worth is volume.
10. Low need means deterministic code, whatever the volume and whatever the program is called.
11. High restraint constrains ownership of the decision, not use of the model. Draft can be delegated when decide cannot.
12. Expect most intake to be deterministic automation in an AI costume. Re-scope it and deliver it. Saying no to AI is what makes the yes credible.
13. Before automating a step, ask which constraint made it necessary. If AI relaxed that constraint, delete the step.
14. AI relaxes reading, drafting, first pass, translation and consistency checking. It does not touch being wrong, accountability or trust.
15. Choose hub and spoke and keep the mandatory waist short enough to recite: the gateway, audit logging to the central sink, identity and secrets, data egress boundaries, the eval gate before production and the dependency register entry. Defend every addition, and leave free everything a domain expert would want to tune.
16. Watch the center of excellence for four failures: bottleneck, ivory tower, demo factory, tollbooth. Pair every mandatory gate with a service you actually provide.
17. Run five intake gates in order and put governance rule-out before cost and latency, never beside them.
18. The larger governed population never reaches intake. Find embedded vendor features through contracts and renewals, find individually adopted tools through expense, identity and network telemetry, ask people what they use rather than whether they use anything, tier what you find by capability rather than intent, and keep the inventory one nobody can be punished for adding to.
19. A platform team needs two consumers to be a platform team. Until then it is an embedded team.
20. Fund showback first, chargeback once cost per outcome is attributable, and never leave the platform to be funded as a side effect of a project.
21. Distinguish playbook, runbook, template, pattern and standard operating procedure. Decide, do, produce, why, obliged.
22. Give every asset an owner, a scope, a jurisdiction, a version, an eval reference and a review date. Deprecation is the stage that keeps the library trustworthy.
23. Promote on three uses by three owners, with the four exceptions. Name assets after the work, never after the model.
24. Design nine production properties in. Auditability, deletability and honest measurability are the three that defeat a retrofit, and reversibility and portability are the two the readiness gate in 8.1 does not test.
